endorsements.title: CHAI Responsible AI Guide (Assurance Standards Guide)
endorsements.quote: In addition, the implementer team should identify whether consent to use patient data has been obtained.

endorsements.title: FUTURE-AI: international consensus guideline for trustworthy and deployable artificial intelligence in healthcare
endorsements.quote: This should be subject to informed consent and approval by ethics committees to ensure an appropriate balance between the benefits of non-discrimination and the risks of reidentification.

endorsements.title: Integrating tumor location into artificial intelligence-based prognostic models in cancer
endorsements.quote: Informed consent must be completed for AI-driven decision making[ 35 ].

commentary.bottom_line: No study supplied tests whether obtaining informed consent before collecting sensitive attributes for fairness assessment or before paired tumor-normal sequencing reduces unconsented data use, and no study documents how often the hazard occurs. The recommendation rests on three endorsements, a framework, a consensus guideline, and a commentary, each stated as a should.

perspectives.view: Zero studies test the practice and zero studies document the hazard, so no certainty rating above no direct evidence is possible. The three endorsements are expert opinion. The FUTURE-AI guideline frames consent as a trade-off between non-discrimination benefits and reidentification risk, but no data were supplied to estimate either side of that balance.

The CHAI guide asks implementers to identify whether consent was obtained, which is a verification step rather than a requirement to collect consent. FUTURE-AI pairs consent with ethics committee approval. The tumor-location commentary extends consent to AI-driven decision making generally. These sources differ in scope, and none cited here has statutory force.

commentary.research_gap: No supplied study measures how often sensitive demographic or genomic data are collected for AI fairness work or tumor-normal sequencing without consent, or whether consent procedures change participation rates, data completeness for fairness audits, or reidentification incidents. Studies comparing consent models, such as broad versus specific consent, on these outcomes would allow a certainty rating.
commentary.underserved_note: No study tested the practice, so no evidence covers Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Consent processes that depend on written English or high literacy may reduce participation from these groups and thin the demographic data that fairness assessments need, but this possibility remains untested in the supplied evidence.
